sources.title: Natsume Sōseki (Q180903), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Natsume Sōseki', description 'Japanese novelist', born 1867-02-09, died 1916-12-09, citizenship Japan, Korean label 나쓰메 소세키. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Natsume Sōseki' (full article read, about 600 words). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: an outstanding Japanese novelist of the Meiji period and the first to ably depict the plight of the alienated modern Japanese intellectual; degree in English from the University of Tokyo in 1893, provincial teaching, government scholarship to England in 1900, lecturer at Tokyo from 1903; fame from I Am a Cat and Botchan, then Kusamakura; after 1907 he gave up teaching to write, producing Mon, Kokoro, Michikusa; says the modern realistic novel took root in Japan through him.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'NATSUME Soseki', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (English biographical note, read in full). Library biography: English department of the Imperial University 1893, teaching, London from 1900, instructor at Tokyo University, debut with I Am a Cat 1905-06, contract storywriter for the Asahi Shimbun from 1907, later novels, an expression style that differed from the naturalists and was called Yoyu-ha, evaluated as one of the great storywriters of modern Japan, and students who became writers. The page hosts the library's portraits of him.

Inoue Yusuke, 'Natsume Soseki: Japan's Foremost Modern Novelist', Nippon.com (Shapers of Japanese History series, 9 February 2017; read in full, about 2,300 words). Detailed popular biography from the Nippon Communications Foundation: studies in classical Chinese and English, the London year of intense study that bore fruit in Theory of Literature, the Thursday meetings with disciples including Akutagawa, the 1907 move from the university to the Asahi Shimbun described as extraordinary at the time, the 1911 refusal of an honorary doctorate, the two trilogies, and later assessments by the translator Damian Flanagan and the scholar Michael K. Bourdaghs (admiring). Passages on his health and mental state were read but are not used.

'Soseki Natsume', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale; read at Encyclopedia.com, about 1,500 words). Reference biography with a critical-literary framing: his command of English and the library of hundreds of English books with his marginal notes, the refusal of uncritical Westernisation, the 1907 decision to give up the security and prestige of a university post for the Asahi, a note that thereafter he spurned official honours, and a survey of the novels. Statements about his nervous condition and the personal interpretation of his late novels were read but are not used.

'Natsume Soseki Chronology (1867-1916)', a dated chronology posted on a university lecturer's personal site (Universitas Gadjah Mada staff blog) and credited there to Marvin Marcus, 'Reflections in a Glass Door' (University of Hawai'i Press, 2009), read in full (about 1,700 words). Used only for dated career facts (April 1907 resignation from the Imperial University and other posts; 3 May 1907 joined the Tokyo Asahi Shinbun as the highest-paid staff writer; the Thursday Society from October 1906; the February 1911 refusal of the Education Ministry's honorary doctorate; annual serialised novels 1907-1916; lectures in 1911 and 1914). The primary book was not opened; the chronology also lists health and family events, which are not used.

Tohoku University Library, 'Natsume Soseki Library' and 'About Natsume Soseki' (two short pages, read in full). The university holds his personal book collection and some of his handwritten works; its biography lists the Asahi serials from 1907 on (Gubijinso through Light and Darkness) and gives his death in 1916.

Marie Omata, 'Natsume Soseki and Arts' (exhibition notice), The Japan Times, 9 May 2013 (read in full, about 150 words). Short notice for an exhibition at the Tokyo University of the Arts museum: says he was a fan of and knowledgeable about Japanese and British art, often referred to painters in his works, and collected more than 200 works by 80 artists.

Wikipedia, 'Natsume Sōseki' (read; orientation only, never counted as a source and not used as support for any row). It was read to check the commonly repeated career claims (Thursday Salon, 1907 move, 1911 honour refused); its extensive passages on his health, mental state and family were deliberately not used.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_soseki_brit, src_soseki_ndl, src_soseki_nippon, src_soseki_gale | 1905-1916 | reference + library + popular biography + critical-literary reference] Britannica calls him the first to ably depict the alienated modern Japanese intellectual and says the modern realistic novel took root in Japan through him; the library says his style differed from the naturalist writers then in vogue; Nippon.com reports a scholar ranking him with pioneers of twentieth-century literature and says his Theory of Literature was among the first works to take a psychological and sociological approach to literature; Gale describes keen psychological insight. These are retrospective assessments written by admirers and encyclopedists, and no sceptical study of his originality was read. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 74 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.58 because every source is retrospective praise and the 'first' and comparison claims are echoed between reference works rather than independently tested.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_soseki_nippon, src_soseki_gale, src_soseki_chron, src_soseki_brit | 1907-1911 | popular biography + critical reference + dated chronology + reference] In April 1907 he resigned from the Imperial University and his other teaching posts and on 3 May joined the Tokyo Asahi Shinbun (the chronology says as its highest-paid staff writer); Nippon.com says the move to full-time writing at the Asahi was regarded at the time as an extraordinary decision, Gale says he gave up the security and prestige of a university professorship and afterwards spurned official honours, and Britannica says he gave up teaching in 1907 to write. The move came with a salaried contract, which limits how far it measures a need for independence from institutions; Nippon.com and the chronology both place a declined state honour in 1911. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): autonomy_need lowered from 72 / 0.62 to 70 / 0.56 because the 1907 resignation is documented, but the supporting framing is popular biography and a chronology rather than independent analysis of his motives.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_soseki_nippon, src_soseki_chron, src_soseki_gale | 1903-1911 | popular biography + chronology + critical reference] Nippon.com says that in 1911 the Education Ministry offered him an honorary doctorate, which he declined, disliking the contemporary spirit of studying merely to acquire such recognition, and the chronology dates the refusal to February 1911; Gale says that although he firmly admired Western literature he did not indulge in slavish imitation of all things foreign and sought to create something of lasting value from the traditions of his own country. The stated reason for the refusal is a one-sentence summary in a single source, so the confidence is moderate.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_soseki_gale, src_soseki_nippon, src_soseki_tohoku, src_soseki_brit | 1884-1916 | critical reference + popular biography + university library + reference] Gale says he mastered English to the point of reading and writing it with great fluency and that at his death his library held hundreds of English-language books with his marginal annotations in English, and Tohoku University Library holds his personal book collection; Nippon.com says he spent every moment of his last London year in study, which later produced Theory of Literature, and that he was learned in classical Chinese from youth. Study habits and a large working library are documented; the independent evaluation of the depth of his scholarship is thin.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_soseki_nippon, src_soseki_gale, src_soseki_jt, src_soseki_chron | 1880s-1916 | popular biography + critical reference + press + chronology] Nippon.com says he was learned in classical Chinese and wrote more than 200 poems and other works in classical Chinese while also becoming a scholar and teacher of English literature; Gale says he combined Western and Japanese traditions in his fiction; the Japan Times says he was knowledgeable about Japanese and British art and collected over 200 works by 80 artists; the chronology records haiku practice, Noh chanting (utai) practice and watercolour painting. The range is wide and well documented, but how well he commanded each field is not independently assessed.

persistence.rationale: [src_soseki_chron, src_soseki_nippon, src_soseki_tohoku | 1907-1916 | chronology + popular biography + university library] After joining the Asahi in 1907 he serialised a major novel almost every year (Gubijinso 1907, Sanshiro 1908, And Then 1909, The Gate 1910, To the Spring Equinox and Beyond and The Wayfarer 1912-13, Kokoro 1914, Grass on the Wayside 1915, Light and Darkness 1916, left unfinished at his death), as the chronology and the university library's list of serials show. The signal is of sustained output under a newspaper commitment; it is read from the list of works alone, and nothing about illness or personal circumstances is used.

portrait.source: Portrait photograph of Natsume Soseki at about 45 in a tweed jacket with a mourning armband, resting his head on his hand, attributed to the photographer Ogawa Kazumasa (1860-1929) and dated September 1912 on the Wikimedia Commons file page 'Natsume Soseki photo.jpg' (Commons gives Jiten.com and a Japan Times page as its sources; the uploader's date is not independently documented). Corroboration read: the Japanese art-magazine Bijutsu Techo's entry on Ogawa Kazumasa calls him the photographer of the portrait that was the original for the Soseki image on the 1,000-yen note, and Toyo Keizai Online says the note portrait is a photograph taken when Soseki was 45 to commemorate the Meiji Emperor's funeral, which matches the visible armband. Rights basis: the creator Ogawa Kazumasa died in 1929 (Wikidata record Q3133048 lists 1860-1929), so a photograph of 1912 had passed out of copyright in Japan long before the 1 January 1996 US restoration date and is in the public domain in the United States as well; Commons tags it as an old Japanese photograph in the public domain. No institutional notice conflicting with this was found: the image is a faithful scan of a 1912 photograph and no museum or publisher reproduction restriction was found for the scan used. Caveats: I could not open a first-publication record for the print, and the Commons file's source pages do not themselves document the authorship, so the photographer attribution rests on the Commons record plus the corroborating Japanese pages. Original 1378 x 1881 pixels, downscaled to 879 x 1200 (no cropping, never upscaled).
portrait.attribution: Photograph attributed to Ogawa Kazumasa, September 1912, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
portrait.creator: Ogawa Kazumasa (1860-1929)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: strong (lead) / CONFIRMED WITH CAVEATS: named photographer with a known death year (1929), PD in Japan before the 1996 US date, mourning armband matches the documented 1912 context; the attribution and September 1912 date rest on the Commons page plus two Japanese corroborating pages (Bijutsu Techo, Toyo Keizai), not on an institutional record of the print, which is recorded as a caveat in portrait.source.
